ENEL 585 – Three-Phase Converters

Topic 12

Dr. Philippe Gray

Department of Electrical & Software Engineering

Three-Phase Converters: The Plan

With no neutral wire and equal inductors, a three-phase converter behaves as two independent single-phase circuits, and Topic 11 already controls one.

  1. What a three-phase set can contain: positive, negative and zero sequence
  2. The circuit: three legs, one inductor per phase, and a neutral that floats
  3. The Clarke transform: from three coupled equations to two independent ones
  4. Control of the two circuits: power, current references and Topic 11’s current loop

Why Three Phases

Balanced sinusoidal voltages and currents, unity power factor

Recall from Topic 8

Balanced set: three sinusoids \(x_{A},x_{B},x_{C}\) with one peak \(\hat X\) and one frequency \(\omega\), each \(2\pi/3\) from the other two:

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{A}&=\hat X\cos\omega t\\ x_{B}&=\hat X\cos\bigl(\omega t-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)\\ x_{C}&=\hat X\cos\bigl(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr) \end{aligned} \]

  1. One phase pulses: \(p_{A}(t)=P+P\cos 2\omega t\), so a single-phase link must buffer \(2\omega\) energy.
  1. Three phases cancel: the three \(2\omega\) terms sum to zero at every instant, so \(p_{t,1}(t)=3P\).
  1. So the dc link sees no \(2\omega\) ripple, as long as the phase voltages and the phase currents are balanced sinusoidal sets at the same frequency and with the same phase order.

Positive, Negative and Zero Sequence

Same peak, same frequency; the order differs. Positive and negative sequence sets are balanced; zero sequence is not.

Any Three-Phase Set Is a Sum of These

Fortescue: any three phasors at one frequency are the sum of one positive, one negative and one zero sequence set.

In symbols, each set named by its phase-\(A\) phasor: \[\begin{aligned} \underline{V}_{A}&=\underline{V}_{+}+\underline{V}_{-}+\underline{V}_{0}\\ \underline{V}_{B}&=\underline{V}_{+}\,1\angle{-120^\circ}+\underline{V}_{-}\,1\angle 120^\circ+\underline{V}_{0}\\ \underline{V}_{C}&=\underline{V}_{+}\,1\angle 120^\circ+\underline{V}_{-}\,1\angle{-120^\circ}+\underline{V}_{0} \end{aligned}\]

The example, peaks at \(0^\circ\): \(\underline{V}_{+}=100\), \(\underline{V}_{-}=40\), \(\underline{V}_{0}=25\) V \[\begin{aligned} \underline{V}_{A}&=100+40+25=165\angle 0^\circ\ \text{V}\\ \underline{V}_{B}&=100\angle{-120^\circ}+40\angle 120^\circ+25=68.7\angle{-130.9^\circ}\ \text{V}\\ \underline{V}_{C}&=100\angle 120^\circ+40\angle{-120^\circ}+25=68.7\angle 130.9^\circ\ \text{V} \end{aligned}\]

Add the three lines: the \(+\) and \(-\) sets each sum to zero, so \(\underline{V}_{0}=\tfrac13\left(\underline{V}_{A}+\underline{V}_{B}+\underline{V}_{C}\right)\); here \(\tfrac13(165-90)=25\) V.

Each Sequence Can Be Solved on Its Own

Linear, with the same \(R\) in every phase

  1. Superposition: split each source into its \(+\), \(-\) and \(0\) parts, solve for each part alone, and add the currents.
  1. Positive sequence alone: the circuit is the same from every phase, so the currents are a positive sequence set too. They sum to zero: \(i_{n}=0\), \(n\) sits at \(N\), and \(\underline{I}_{+}=\underline{V}_{+}/R\).
  1. Negative sequence alone: the same with \(B\) and \(C\) swapped, so \(\underline{I}_{-}=\underline{V}_{-}/R\).
  1. Zero sequence alone: three equal currents \(\underline{I}_{0}\), so \(\underline{I}_{n}=3\underline{I}_{0}\) and \(\underline{V}_{0}=(R+3R_{n})\,\underline{I}_{0}\).
  1. So three single-phase circuits (below), one per sequence; only the zero sequence sees \(R_{n}\). With no neutral wire, \(R_{n}\to\infty\) and \(\underline{I}_{0}=0\).

Zero Sequence Needs a Return Path

What a missing neutral removes, at each instant

From here on, instantaneous values: KCL and KVL hold at every instant, for any waveforms; phasors hold only for steady-state sinusoids.

Zero sequence current: \(i_{0}=\tfrac13\left(i_{A}+i_{B}+i_{C}\right)\), the part all three phases carry equally.

  1. KCL at \(n\): \(i_{A}+i_{B}+i_{C}=0\) at every instant.
  1. So \(i_{0}=0\): no zero sequence current flows.
  1. A zero sequence voltage can still exist: added to all three sources, it moves \(n\) with respect to \(N\) and drives no current.

The Clarke Transform

At each instant, for any waveforms; \(x\) is a voltage or a current:

\[\begin{bmatrix}x_{\alpha}\\x_{\beta}\\x_{0}\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\tfrac23\begin{bmatrix}1&-\tfrac12&-\tfrac12\\0&\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}&-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\tfrac12&\tfrac12&\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{T}}\begin{bmatrix}x_{A}\\x_{B}\\x_{C}\end{bmatrix}\]

What each row computes

  1. Row 3, the mean of the three: \(x_{0}=\tfrac13\left(x_{A}+x_{B}+x_{C}\right)\), the zero sequence part.
  1. Row 1, phase \(A\) less the mean: \(x_{\alpha}=x_{A}-x_{0}\).
  1. Row 2, the \(B\) to \(C\) difference: \(x_{\beta}=\dfrac{x_{B}-x_{C}}{\sqrt3}\).
  1. Rows 1 and 2 each sum to zero: adding the same value to all three inputs leaves \(x_{\alpha}\) and \(x_{\beta}\) unchanged; it shows only in \(x_{0}\).

Clarke on the Resistor Circuit

\[\begin{bmatrix}v_{A}\\v_{B}\\v_{C}\end{bmatrix}=R\begin{bmatrix}i_{A}\\i_{B}\\i_{C}\end{bmatrix}+v_{nN}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}\]

KVL round each phase; \(v_{nN}\): \(n\) with respect to \(N\)

Three coupled equations become two independent ones

  1. Multiply both sides by \(\mathbf{T}\). Each set of three becomes its \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(0\) values. \(R\) is the same in each phase, so it comes outside: \[\begin{bmatrix}v_{\alpha}\\v_{\beta}\\v_{0}\end{bmatrix}=R\begin{bmatrix}i_{\alpha}\\i_{\beta}\\i_{0}\end{bmatrix}+v_{nN}\,\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}\]

  1. The last term: \(v_{nN}\) is the same in all three phases, so only the \(0\) row keeps it:

    \[\begin{bmatrix}v_{\alpha}\\v_{\beta}\\v_{0}\end{bmatrix}=R\begin{bmatrix}i_{\alpha}\\i_{\beta}\\i_{0}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\v_{nN}\end{bmatrix}\]

    \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\): two single-phase circuits.
    \(0\): KCL at \(n\) gives \(i_{A}+i_{B}+i_{C}=0\), so \(i_{0}=0\) and \(v_{0}=v_{nN}\).

Worked Example: Clarke and Back

Example, at one instant:
\(\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}v_{A}\\v_{B}\\v_{C}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\4\\-2\end{bmatrix}\text{ V},\quad R=2\ \Omega\)

  1. Clarke: \(\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}v_{\alpha}\\v_{\beta}\\v_{0}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}10\\4\\-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6\\2\sqrt3\\4\end{bmatrix}\text{ V}\)
  1. Solve, \(i_{0}=0\): \(\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}i_{\alpha}\\i_{\beta}\\i_{0}\end{bmatrix}=\frac1R\begin{bmatrix}v_{\alpha}\\v_{\beta}\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\\sqrt3\\0\end{bmatrix}\text{ A}\)
  1. Back, \(\mathbf{T}^{-1}\): \(\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}i_{A}\\i_{B}\\i_{C}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\-\tfrac12&\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}&1\\-\tfrac12&-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\\sqrt3\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\0\\-3\end{bmatrix}\text{ A}\)
  1. Check, KVL with \(v_{nN}=v_{0}\): \(\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}i_{A}\\i_{B}\\i_{C}\end{bmatrix}=\frac1R\begin{bmatrix}10-4\\4-4\\-2-4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\0\\-3\end{bmatrix}\text{ A}\)

From Two Probes to α and β

No neutral access is needed

  1. Measure two line-to-line voltages: \(v_{AB}\) and \(v_{BC}\).
  1. Write Clarke’s α and β rows as differences: \[\begin{aligned}v_{\alpha}&=\tfrac13\left(2v_{A}-v_{B}-v_{C}\right)=\frac{2v_{AB}+v_{BC}}{3}\\v_{\beta}&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(v_{B}-v_{C}\right)=\frac{v_{BC}}{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}\]
  1. Exact for any three voltages: \(v_{\alpha}\) and \(v_{\beta}\) hold no zero sequence, and neither do line-to-line voltages.

A Balanced Set Becomes a Cosine and a Sine

Positive sequence, peak \(\hat X\): \(x_{A}=\hat X\cos\omega t\), \(x_{B}=\hat X\cos\bigl(\omega t-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)\), \(x_{C}=\hat X\cos\bigl(\omega t+\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr)\)

What \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are for a balanced set

  1. The phases sum to zero, so \(x_{0}=0\) and \(x_{\alpha}=x_{A}=\hat X\cos\omega t\).
  1. The \(B\) to \(C\) difference: \(x_{B}-x_{C}=2\hat X\sin\omega t\,\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sqrt3\,\hat X\sin\omega t\), so \(x_{\beta}=\hat X\sin\omega t\).
  1. Both have the phase peak \(\hat X\), \(x_{\beta}\) lagging \(x_{\alpha}\) by \(90^\circ\). That is the \(\tfrac23\) in \(\mathbf{T}\): without it, both peaks would be \(\tfrac32\hat X\).
  1. Negative sequence, \(B\) and \(C\) swapped: \(x_{\alpha}\) is unchanged and \(x_{\beta}=-\hat X\sin\omega t\). So \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) carry both sequences; Clarke does not separate them.

Positive Sequence: One Point on a Circle

Plot \((x_{\alpha},x_{\beta})\) as a point, read off the waveforms at the cursor. The arrow from the origin to it is the space vector \(\vec x_{\alpha\beta}\).

Balanced positive sequence: \(x_{\alpha}^{2}+x_{\beta}^{2}=\hat X^{2}\left(\cos^{2}\omega t+\sin^{2}\omega t\right)=\hat X^{2}\): a circle of radius \(\hat X\), counter-clockwise at \(\omega\).

Three Legs Into a Grid

Topic 8’s bridge, with Topic 11’s inductor and grid in each phase

Still no phasors: they give only the steady state, and control needs how the currents change, so we average over \(T_{s}\), as in Topic 11.

What the switches control

  1. One leg: top switch on, \(v_{tAN}=+v_{d}/2\); bottom switch on, \(v_{tAN}=-v_{d}/2\).
  1. Average over \(T_{s}\) (\(f_{s}\gg f_{1}\)): \[\langle v_{tAN}\rangle_{T_{s}}=m_{A}\frac{\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_{s}}}{2},\quad m_{A}=2d_{A}-1\] \(d_{A}\): fraction of \(T_{s}\) with \(S_{1}\) on. \(m_{A}\): leg \(A\)’s modulation, from \(-1\) (\(S_{2}\) always on) to \(+1\) (\(S_{1}\) always on).
  1. Half Topic 11’s gain: a leg swings \(\pm v_{d}/2\); the bridge swung \(\pm v_{d}\).
  1. \(N\) is a reference, so the link need not be split. \(n\) floats: nothing ties it to \(N\), as on the resistor circuit.

Three References, One Carrier

Sine-triangle PWM on three legs

  1. One carrier, three references: \(m_{A}\), \(m_{B}\), \(m_{C}\), \(120^\circ\) apart, each of peak \(m_{i}\).
  1. Each leg: \(v_{tAN}\), \(v_{tBN}\), \(v_{tCN}\) are each \(\pm v_{d}/2\), with fundamentals of peak \(m_{i}v_{d}/2\) (red).
  1. Line to line: \(v_{AB}=v_{tAN}-v_{tBN}\) and \(v_{BC}=v_{tBN}-v_{tCN}\) take \(0\) or \(\pm v_{d}\), with fundamentals of peak \(\sqrt{3}\,m_{i}v_{d}/2\).
  1. The limit: for \(m_{i}\le 1\), a phase’s fundamental peak is at most \(v_{d}/2\). The control slides return to this.

Shown: \(m_{i}=0.8\), \(f_{s}=15f_{1}\)

KVL, Phase by Phase

Round phase \(A\), from \(N\) to \(n\) and back

  1. Follow the loop: \[v_{tAN}=L\frac{di_{LA}}{dt}+v_{gA}+v_{nN}\]
  1. All three phases: \[\begin{aligned} L\frac{di_{LA}}{dt}&=v_{tAN}-v_{nN}-v_{gA}\\ L\frac{di_{LB}}{dt}&=v_{tBN}-v_{nN}-v_{gB}\\ L\frac{di_{LC}}{dt}&=v_{tCN}-v_{nN}-v_{gC} \end{aligned}\]
  1. Topic 11’s equation plus one term. We chose the legs; \(v_{nN}\) we did not.

Where the Neutral Sits

Shown: one \(T_{s}\) at \(\omega t=15^\circ\), \(m_{i}=0.8\)

Add the three equations

\[\begin{aligned} L\frac{d}{dt}\left(i_{LA}+i_{LB}+i_{LC}\right)&=v_{tAN}+v_{tBN}+v_{tCN}\\ &\quad-3v_{nN}-\left(v_{gA}+v_{gB}+v_{gC}\right) \end{aligned}\]

  1. No wire from \(n\), equal \(L\): KCL at \(n\) gives \(i_{LA}+i_{LB}+i_{LC}=0\), so the left side is \(0\).
  1. Balanced grid: \(v_{gA}+v_{gB}+v_{gC}=0\), so the last bracket is \(0\).
  1. What is left: \[v_{nN}=\frac{v_{tAN}+v_{tBN}+v_{tCN}}{3}\] It moves in steps of \(v_{d}/3\).
  1. So each phase’s current depends on all three legs, through \(v_{nN}\). Next: Clarke, as on the resistor circuit.

Clarke on the Converter

Start: the three KVL equations

\[\begin{aligned} L\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix}i_{LA}\\i_{LB}\\i_{LC}\end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix}v_{tAN}\\v_{tBN}\\v_{tCN}\end{bmatrix}\\ &\quad-v_{nN}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}v_{gA}\\v_{gB}\\v_{gC}\end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}\]

Equal \(L\) in the three phases, no neutral wire, balanced grid

The resistor circuit’s steps, with \(L\,d/dt\) in place of \(R\)

  1. Multiply both sides by \(\mathbf{T}\). Each set of three becomes its \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(0\) values. \(\mathbf{T}\) is constant and \(L\) is the same in each phase, so \(L\,d/dt\) comes outside, and \(\mathbf{T}\) maps \((1,1,1)\) to \((0,0,1)\) as before: \[L\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix}i_{L\alpha}\\i_{L\beta}\\i_{L0}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{t\alpha}\\v_{t\beta}\\v_{t0}\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\v_{nN}\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}v_{g\alpha}\\v_{g\beta}\\v_{g0}\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. The \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) rows: \(v_{nN}\) has dropped out: \[L\frac{di_{L\alpha}}{dt}=v_{t\alpha}-v_{g\alpha},\qquad L\frac{di_{L\beta}}{dt}=v_{t\beta}-v_{g\beta}\]
  1. The \(0\) row: \(i_{L0}=0\) (no neutral wire) and \(v_{g0}=0\) (balanced grid), so \(v_{nN}=v_{t0}\): the mean of the three legs, as on the last slide.

Two Single-Phase Circuits

The circuit each equation describes, and the goal

  1. Topic 11’s circuit, once per axis: \(L\,di_{L}/dt=v_{t}-v_{g}\).
  1. A balanced positive sequence grid, peak \(\hat V_{g}\), gives a cosine and a sine: \(v_{g\alpha}=\hat V_{g}\cos\omega t\), \(v_{g\beta}=\hat V_{g}\sin\omega t\).
  1. These are calculations, not wires: the legs still carry \(A\), \(B\), \(C\). We compute \(v_{t\alpha}\), \(v_{t\beta}\), then the inverse gives the legs.
  1. The goal: deliver a chosen \(P^{*}\) and \(Q_{g}^{*}\), totals for the three phases, by choosing \(v_{t\alpha}\) and \(v_{t\beta}\).
  1. Topic 11 controls one such circuit. One thing differs: each leg’s gain is \(v_{d}/2\), half the H-bridge’s \(v_{d}\), so with sine PWM \(v_{t\alpha}\) and \(v_{t\beta}\) reach at most \(v_{d}/2\) peak, where the H-bridge reached \(v_{d}\).

Power from α and β

Start: power into the grid, at each instant

\[p=v_{gA}i_{LA}+v_{gB}i_{LB}+v_{gC}i_{LC}\]

Each phase from its \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(0\) values, by \(\mathbf{T}^{-1}\):

\[\begin{aligned}x_{A}&=x_{\alpha}+x_{0}\\x_{B}&=-\tfrac12x_{\alpha}+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}x_{\beta}+x_{0}\\x_{C}&=-\tfrac12x_{\alpha}-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}x_{\beta}+x_{0}\end{aligned}\]

Substitute for \(v_{g}\) and \(i_{L}\)

  1. Collect terms: the cross terms cancel, leaving \[p=\tfrac32\left(v_{g\alpha}i_{L\alpha}+v_{g\beta}i_{L\beta}\right)+3v_{g0}i_{L0}\]
  1. No neutral wire, so \(i_{L0}=0\) and, for any waveforms, \[p=\tfrac32\begin{bmatrix}v_{g\alpha}&v_{g\beta}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}i_{L\alpha}\\i_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}\]

  1. Positive sequence, steady state: currents of peak \(\hat I_{L}\), lagging \(v_{g}\) by \(\varphi\): \[\begin{bmatrix}i_{L\alpha}\\i_{L\beta}\\i_{L0}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}i_{LA}\\i_{LB}\\i_{LC}\end{bmatrix}=\hat I_{L}\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t-\varphi)\\\sin(\omega t-\varphi)\\0\end{bmatrix}\]

    \[p=\tfrac32\hat V_{g}\hat I_{L}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t-\varphi)\\\sin(\omega t-\varphi)\end{bmatrix}=\tfrac32\hat V_{g}\hat I_{L}\cos\varphi=P\]

  1. No \(2\omega\) power at the dc link, unlike Topic 11; negative sequence adds it.

Reactive Power in α and β

One instant: \(\vec v_{g\alpha\beta}=(v_{g\alpha},v_{g\beta})\), length \(\hat V_{g}\), and \(\vec i_{L\alpha\beta}=(i_{L\alpha},i_{L\beta})\), length \(\hat I_{L}\). Both turn at \(\omega\); \(\varphi\) stays fixed.

The current’s part across the voltage

  1. Define, at each instant: \[q=\tfrac32\begin{bmatrix}v_{g\beta}&-v_{g\alpha}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}i_{L\alpha}\\i_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. Positive sequence, steady state, the current lagging by \(\varphi\): \[\begin{aligned}q&=\tfrac32\hat V_{g}\hat I_{L}\begin{bmatrix}\sin\omega t&-\cos\omega t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t-\varphi)\\\sin(\omega t-\varphi)\end{bmatrix}\\&=\tfrac32\hat V_{g}\hat I_{L}\sin\varphi=Q_{g}\end{aligned}\] positive for a lagging current, as in Topic 6.
  1. Constant in time, like \(p\): no \(\omega t\) is left. A negative sequence part in the grid voltages or the currents adds a \(2\omega\) part to both.

The Current Reference from the Wanted Power

\(p\) and \(q\) as one matrix equation

\[\begin{bmatrix}p\\q\end{bmatrix}=\tfrac32\,\mathbf{M}(t)\begin{bmatrix}i_{L\alpha}\\i_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}\] \[\mathbf{M}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}v_{g\alpha}(t)&v_{g\beta}(t)\\v_{g\beta}(t)&-v_{g\alpha}(t)\end{bmatrix}\]

\(\mathbf{M}(t)\) changes with time: its entries are the grid voltages at that instant.

Invert, at each instant: \(\mathbf{M}(t)^{2}=\left(v_{g\alpha}^{2}+v_{g\beta}^{2}\right)\mathbf{I}\), so for \(v_{g\alpha}^{2}+v_{g\beta}^{2}>0\) \[\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{3\left(v_{g\alpha}^{2}+v_{g\beta}^{2}\right)}\,\mathbf{M}(t)\begin{bmatrix}P^{*}\\Q_{g}^{*}\end{bmatrix}\]

Building the reference

  1. Positive sequence grid, peak \(\hat V_{g}\): \(v_{g\alpha}^{2}+v_{g\beta}^{2}=\hat V_{g}^{2}\), a constant, and \[\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{3\hat V_{g}}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t\\\sin\omega t&-\cos\omega t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P^{*}\\Q_{g}^{*}\end{bmatrix}\] Constant commands give sinusoidal references.
  1. With a PLL, as in Topic 11: it tracks the grid voltage’s angle \(\omega t\) and, in steady state, outputs \(\cos\omega t\), \(\sin\omega t\) and \(\hat V_{g}\): the entries of step 1.
  1. Without one: use the measured \(v_{g\alpha}\), \(v_{g\beta}\) (slide 11’s probes) in \(\mathbf{M}(t)\) directly. A distorted or unbalanced grid then passes into the reference.

Worked Example: Current Reference

Solve for the current references \(i^{*}_{L\alpha}\), \(i^{*}_{L\beta}\)

Inputs: \(\hat V_{g}=169.7\) V (120/208 V grid) \(P^{*}=5.09\) kW \(Q_{g}^{*}=0\) \(\omega t=30^\circ\), then \(120^\circ\)

  1. At \(\omega t=30^\circ\), slide 22’s matrix: \[\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{3(169.7)}\begin{bmatrix}\cos30^\circ&\sin30^\circ\\\sin30^\circ&-\cos30^\circ\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5090\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}17.32\\10.00\end{bmatrix}\text{ A}\]
  1. At \(\omega t=120^\circ\): \[\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{3(169.7)}\begin{bmatrix}\cos120^\circ&\sin120^\circ\\\sin120^\circ&-\cos120^\circ\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5090\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10.00\\17.32\end{bmatrix}\text{ A}\] Still 20 A long, turned \(90^\circ\) with \(\omega t\): the reference rotates.

Three Leg Modulations in α and β

Start: the three legs, averaged (slide 14)

\[\begin{bmatrix}\langle v_{tAN}\rangle_{T_s}\\\langle v_{tBN}\rangle_{T_s}\\\langle v_{tCN}\rangle_{T_s}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}m_{A}\\m_{B}\\m_{C}\end{bmatrix}\]

One dc link, so the same \(\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}\) in every leg

The three legs’ \(m_{A}\), \(m_{B}\), \(m_{C}\) against the carrier (slide 15): \(m_{i}=0.8\), \(f_{s}=15f_{1}\)

Slide 18’s step: multiply by \(\mathbf{T}\)

  1. \(\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}/2\) is one number, so it comes outside \(\mathbf{T}\): \[\begin{bmatrix}\langle v_{t\alpha}\rangle_{T_s}\\\langle v_{t\beta}\rangle_{T_s}\\\langle v_{t0}\rangle_{T_s}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}m_{\alpha}\\m_{\beta}\\m_{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad\begin{bmatrix}m_{\alpha}\\m_{\beta}\\m_{0}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}m_{A}\\m_{B}\\m_{C}\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. So, for commands \(v^{*}_{t\alpha}\), \(v^{*}_{t\beta}\): \[m_{\alpha}=\frac{v^{*}_{t\alpha}}{\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}/2},\qquad m_{\beta}=\frac{v^{*}_{t\beta}}{\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}/2}\] \(m_{0}\) sets only \(v_{nN}\) and drives no current (slide 18).

The Same Loop, Twice

Topic 11’s loop on each axis

  1. Each axis is Topic 11’s plant: \(L\,d\langle i_{L\alpha}\rangle_{T_s}/dt=\langle v_{t\alpha}\rangle_{T_s}-\langle v_{g\alpha}\rangle_{T_s}\), the same for \(\beta\).
  1. Prediction plus correction: \(v^{*}_{t\alpha}=\langle v_{g\alpha}\rangle_{T_s}+L\,di^{*}_{L\alpha}/dt+v_{c\alpha}\), with the PR output \(v_{c\alpha}=G_{c}(s)e_{\alpha}\).
  1. The one change, the modulator: \(2/\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}\) (slide 24), where Topic 11 had \(1/\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}\). It cancels the legs’ \(\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}/2\).
  1. So \(T(s)=G_{c}(s)/(sL)\) on each axis, as in Topic 11.

Turning a Pair by δ: the Rotation Matrix

\(\delta\) is drawn as \(35^\circ\) to be seen; the example’s is \(1.6^\circ\).

The pair a time \(\tau\) later, from the pair now

  1. A positive sequence pair is a point on a circle (slide 13): \(x_{\alpha}=\hat X\cos\omega t\), \(x_{\beta}=\hat X\sin\omega t\).
  1. A time \(\tau\) later it is at \(\omega t+\delta\), with \(\delta=\omega\tau\). Expand: \[\begin{aligned}\hat X\cos(\omega t+\delta)&=x_{\alpha}\cos\delta-x_{\beta}\sin\delta\\\hat X\sin(\omega t+\delta)&=x_{\alpha}\sin\delta+x_{\beta}\cos\delta\end{aligned}\]
  1. As a matrix: \[\begin{bmatrix}x_{\alpha}(t+\tau)\\x_{\beta}(t+\tau)\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\cos\delta&-\sin\delta\\\sin\delta&\cos\delta\end{bmatrix}}_{R(\delta)}\begin{bmatrix}x_{\alpha}(t)\\x_{\beta}(t)\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. Only \(\delta\) is needed, not \(\hat X\) or \(\omega t\): \(R(\delta)\) keeps the length and turns any positive sequence pair counter-clockwise by \(\delta\).

Feedforward in α and β

The reference’s slope, without differentiating

  1. The reference (slide 22): \[\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{3\hat V_{g}}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\omega t&\sin\omega t\\\sin\omega t&-\cos\omega t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P^{*}\\Q_{g}^{*}\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. Constant commands, positive sequence grid of constant amplitude: the reference turns at \(\omega\) like the space vector, so \[\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix}i^{*}_{L\alpha}\\i^{*}_{L\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\omega\begin{bmatrix}-i^{*}_{L\beta}\\i^{*}_{L\alpha}\end{bmatrix}\]
  1. This is Topic 11’s \(L\,di^{*}/dt\) term, read off the reference itself.

Compensate the delay \(\tau\)

  1. The command acts about \(\tau\) after its sample (Topic 11), so both feedforward terms, \(v_{g}\) and \(L\,di^{*}/dt\) (step 3), are wanted at \(t+\tau\).
  1. Both pairs turn at \(\omega\), so \(\tau\) later each is turned by \(R(\delta)\), \(\delta=\omega\tau\) (slide 26): \[\begin{bmatrix}v_{\alpha,\mathrm{ff}}\\v_{\beta,\mathrm{ff}}\end{bmatrix}=R(\delta)\left(\begin{bmatrix}v_{g\alpha}\\v_{g\beta}\end{bmatrix}+\omega L\begin{bmatrix}-i^{*}_{L\beta}\\i^{*}_{L\alpha}\end{bmatrix}\right)\] then \(v^{*}_{t\alpha}=v_{\alpha,\mathrm{ff}}+v_{c\alpha}\), the same for \(\beta\).
  1. Example: \(\tau=1.5T_{s}=75\ \mu\)s at 60 Hz gives \(\delta=1.6^\circ\).

Back to Three Legs

As implemented: the reference (slide 22), the loop on each axis (slide 25) and the feedforward (slide 27), then \(\mathbf{T}^{-1}\) and \(2/\langle v_{d}\rangle_{T_s}\) per leg.

Verifying the Controller

Pale bands: the commands. Averaged model of the example: sampled at the valley, updated the next period (\(\tau\approx1.5T_{s}\)); Topic 11’s PR (\(K_{p}=6.28\ \Omega\), \(K_{r}=10K_{p}\), \(f_{b}=5\) Hz); legs clamped to \(\lvert m_{k}\rvert\le1\)

A ramp of \(P^{*}\), then of \(Q_{g}^{*}\)

  1. 0 to 17 ms: 10 A peak at \(P^{*}=2.545\) kW; \(i_{L\alpha}\), \(i_{L\beta}\) run inside \(i^{*}_{L\alpha}\), \(i^{*}_{L\beta}\), and the errors \(e_{\alpha}=i^{*}_{L\alpha}-i_{L\alpha}\) and \(e_{\beta}\) stay near 0.
  1. 17 to 33 ms, \(P^{*}\) ramps to 5.09 kW: the references grow to 20 A; \(p\) follows the ramp, with errors below 0.1 A.
  1. 67 to 83 ms, \(Q_{g}^{*}\) ramps to 2.55 kvar: the references fall 26.6° behind \(v_{g}\) and rise to 22.4 A; \(q\) follows while \(p\) stays at 5.09 kW.
  1. No leg reaches its limit: the largest requested \(\lvert m_{k}\rvert\) is 0.87, below 1.

Multilevel Preview

Three-level leg (neutral point clamped): \(S_{1}\) to \(S_{4}\) in series, two clamp diodes to \(N\), so \(v_{tAN}\) takes \(+v_{d}/2\), \(0\) or \(-v_{d}/2\). Each switch blocks \(v_{d}/2\) and each step is half the two-level one, for the same fundamental (red; \(m_{i}=0.8\), \(f_{s}=15f_{1}\)).

A preview only: none of the projects uses it.

Three-Level Leg: Switch States

At \(0\) the current picks the clamp diode: with \(S_{2}\), \(S_{3}\) on, \(i_{LA}>0\) flows from \(N\) through \(D_{1}\) and \(S_{2}\), and \(i_{LA}<0\) through \(S_{3}\) and \(D_{2}\) back to \(N\).

Two gate signals: \(S_{3}\) is the complement of \(S_{1}\), \(S_{4}\) of \(S_{2}\). Of the four \((S_{1},S_{2})\) pairs, \(S_{1}\) on with \(S_{2}\) off leaves \(A\) unconnected, so it is not used.

Three-Level Leg: Two Carriers

Shown: \(m_{i}=0.8\), \(f_{s}=15f_{1}\)

Which state, when

  1. Two carriers, one above the other: the upper between \(0\) and \(1\), the lower between \(-1\) and \(0\); \(m_{A}\) as on slide 15.
  1. While \(m_{A}>0\): above the upper carrier \(S_{1}S_{2}\) (\(+v_{d}/2\)), below it \(S_{2}S_{3}\) (\(0\)). \(S_{2}\) stays on and \(S_{1}\) switches.
  1. While \(m_{A}<0\): above the lower carrier \(S_{2}S_{3}\) (\(0\)), below it \(S_{3}S_{4}\) (\(-v_{d}/2\)). \(S_{3}\) stays on and \(S_{4}\) switches.
  1. Average over a carrier period: \(\langle v_{tAN}\rangle=m_{A}v_{d}/2\), as for the two-level leg, so \(m_{k}=2v^{*}_{tkN}/v_{d}\) (slide 28) still holds.

Three-Phase Neutral-Point-Clamped Inverter

Three legs, one split link: every leg’s clamp diodes meet at the same \(N\), so each \(v_{tkN}\) is \(+v_{d}/2\), \(0\) or \(-v_{d}/2\): \(3^{3}=27\) switch states, against \(2^{3}=8\) for the two-level bridge (slide 14).

Line to line: \(v_{AB}=v_{tAN}-v_{tBN}\) takes five levels, \(0\), \(\pm v_{d}/2\), \(\pm v_{d}\), against three for the two-level bridge (slide 15).

What it adds: the current out of \(N\) is the sum of \(i_{Lk}\) over the legs at \(0\); unless it averages to zero, the two capacitor voltages drift from \(v_{d}/2\), so the modulator must also balance them.

Summary

Three phases, two circuits, Topic 11’s loop twice

  1. Sequences: three sinusoids at one frequency are a sum of positive, negative and zero sequence sets; with no neutral wire, no zero sequence current flows.
  2. Clarke: with no neutral wire and equal \(L\), \(v_{nN}\) drops out, leaving two independent circuits; two line-to-line probes give \(v_{g\alpha}\), \(v_{g\beta}\).
  3. Power: \(p=\tfrac32\left(v_{g\alpha}i_{L\alpha}+v_{g\beta}i_{L\beta}\right)\) and \(q=\tfrac32\left(v_{g\beta}i_{L\alpha}-v_{g\alpha}i_{L\beta}\right)\), constant for positive sequence sinusoids; inverting them gives \(i^{*}_{L\alpha}\), \(i^{*}_{L\beta}\).
  4. Control: Topic 11’s PR loop on each axis, its feedforward turned by \(R(\omega\tau)\), then \(\mathbf{T}^{-1}\) and \(m_{k}=2v^{*}_{tkN}/v_{d}\).
